What

What Counts as a Dangerous or Dead Tree

Dangerous-tree designation typically applies when one or more conditions are present: a fully dead trunk with no leaf-out for a full growing season; a significant lean change (more than 5° from the prior year, often visible at the root flare); large dead branches over a target such as a house, driveway, or a neighbor's structure; cavity decay at the trunk base or major branch unions; recent root-plate movement after a windstorm; or ash trees with EAB exit holes and more than 50% canopy thinning.

The work is scaled to that condition rather than to a healthy removal. Dead wood shatters instead of dropping cleanly, climbers cannot trust limb anchorage, and crane support becomes the default rather than the exception. Every dangerous or dead removal Aaron walks starts with a free written estimate and confirmed pricing before any work begins — plus a photo-and-scope package when the removal is insurance-related.

Why

Four Reasons NE Ohio Homeowners Call Roubic

The dangerous- and dead-tree scenarios Aaron walks most often across NE Ohio properties.

EAB-Killed Ash on the Property

Emerald ash borer has killed an estimated 90%+ of NE Ohio ash. Dead ash turns brittle within 18–24 months and fails violently in storms.

Cavity Decay Over a Target

A heritage oak with major cavity decay above a roofline can no longer be trusted for standing-tree work — it needs a controlled, rigged takedown.

Storm Lean / Root-Plate Failure

A maple that shifted after a windstorm has a compromised root plate. Leaning trees over structures need proactive removal before the next storm.

Insurance-Precipitated Removal

When a dead tree falls on a covered structure during a storm, removal of that tree is typically covered — and we document the scope for the claim.

Common Hazard-Tree Questions

Dangerous & Dead Tree Removal FAQ

Five things NE Ohio homeowners want to know before booking.

How do I know if my tree is dangerous?
Look for dead branches in the canopy that don't leaf out in spring; a visible lean change at the base; cavity decay; mushrooms or fungal conks at the trunk; or recent root-plate movement after a storm. A free on-site assessment is the surest way to know — Roubic's lead tech walks the property and documents what we find.
How much does dead tree removal cost in NE Ohio?
Dead tree removal carries a 15–30% premium over live-tree pricing because of brittle-wood complications. Small dead trees (under 20 ft) start around $300–$600; mature dead trees (50–80 ft) run $1,800–$4,000; heritage dead trees requiring crane support can exceed $10,000. See the Tree Service Cost Guide and Tree Removal Cost Calculator for benchmarks.
Will my homeowners insurance pay to remove a dead tree?
Generally no — insurance typically only covers tree removal when a tree damages a covered structure such as a house, garage, fence, or vehicle. Removal of standing dead trees that haven't damaged anything is a homeowner expense. The exception: if the dead tree falls on a covered structure during a covered loss event, removal of that specific tree is typically covered.
How quickly can Roubic remove a dangerous tree?
Active hazards — visibly leaning, root-plate failure, or blocking access — get priority dispatch, often the next day. Standing dead trees that are not actively threatening property typically schedule within 1–3 business days. 24/7 emergency line: {{global.phone}}.
What about EAB-killed ash trees?
EAB has killed an estimated 90%+ of ash trees in NE Ohio since the 2008–2012 outbreak. EAB-killed ash become brittle within 18–24 months of death and fail violently in storms. Plan removal once exit holes appear and canopy thinning exceeds 50%; chemical treatment is no longer cost-effective at that stage. Roubic's wood enters our Auburn Township firewood yard for seasoning.
